analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin prices at international reference levels for federal health programs and all buyers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Health and Human Services Secretary to set an annual maximum insulin price, based on what insulin sells for in eleven other wealthy countries. That cap would apply not only to Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA, and other federal health programs, but to every buyer in the country, including uninsured people paying cash. Drug makers charging more would face penalties equal to ten times the excess.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 30 million Americans with diabetes, especially seniors on Medicare, military families and veterans, people with Medicaid or Indian Health Service coverage, and the uninsured, all of whom would pay no more than the median price in comparable countries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with diabetes, especially seniors and the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: HHS must set an annual insulin reference price based on the median price in countries like Japan, Germany, Canada, and Australia, and no sale could exceed it [S3].
The cap applies to Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA, federal employee coverage, and Indian Health Service programs [S3].
It also applies to everyone outside those programs: manufacturers must offer insulin at the reference price to all individuals, including the uninsured and people with private insurance [S3].
Manufacturers that overcharge face a civil penalty each year equal to ten times the amount they collected above the reference price [S3].
Penalty money would go half to Medicare trust funds and half to the National Institutes of Health for drug research [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers (Novo Nordisk, Sanofi, Eli Lilly) would give up excess profits above international prices; the penalty would otherwise be passed through to no one but shareholders.

drawbacks.text: Capping prices at foreign medians could reduce insulin makers' revenue, which opponents argue could dampen investment in future diabetes treatments; the bill itself acknowledges the tradeoff by requiring HHS to consider manufacturers' research and development costs when no foreign pricing data is available [S3].
The cap applies only to insulin, so it would not help patients priced out of other essential drugs, and there is no comparable bill for other drug classes [S1].
International reference pricing is untested in the U.S. and could face administrative and legal challenges over how HHS compares prices across countries with different dosage conventions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and immediate for insulin users, since the bill directly limits what they pay at the pharmacy, including uninsured cash buyers. The cost falls on a small set of manufacturers rather than being spread across taxpayers, and the main risk is uncertain long-term effects on drug development investment. On balance the design is straightforward and enforceable, with the main gap being that it covers insulin only.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to six House committees, then assigned to a health subcommittee, and none of them ever acted on it, so it never reached a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced December 9, 2019 by Rep. Joyce Beatty with 22 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S4].

The Speaker referred it to six committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Reform, and Natural Resources — a practice that often signals a bill will be parked rather than prioritized [S5].
Subcommittees on Health and on Indigenous Peoples received referrals in December 2019 and January 2020, but no hearings, markups, or votes are recorded [S5].
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers keep charging U.S. prices well above what the same products sell for in other wealthy countries; patients and federal health programs keep paying the difference.

for.name: Rep. Joyce Beatty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap insulin prices at international reference levels.

for.name: 22 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — 23 Democrats including the sponsor and no Republicans — and the record shows no recorded votes because the bill never left committee [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Brand-name insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: Their U.S. insulin prices would be capped at the median of eleven foreign countries and they would face penalties up to ten times any overcharge, eliminating the premium pricing U.S. patients currently pay. Patients and federal programs currently absorb that premium.
Reduced insulin revenue could lower reinvestment in diabetes research; penalty proceeds routed to NIH would partially offset this by funding drug R&D directly.
